newsitem.title: USA: Dole prepares at Florida condo for crucial debate.
newsitem.headline: Dole prepares at Florida condo for crucial debate.

text.p: Bob Dole, struggling to catch up with President Bill Clinton, studied briefing papers and worked on his tan in this palm-dotted playground on Friday, preparing for the critical first presidential debate.
A Dole aide said the Republican challenger planned to spend all day preparing for his debate with Clinton a week from Sunday in Hartford, Connecticut.

The two candidates' camps have been arguing over details such as the form of the podium and the starting time as they jockey for position. The second and last presidential debate is scheduled for Oct. 16 in San Diego.
How important are the encounters for Dole, whom polls have consistently shown lagging far behind Clinton in the last stage of the presidential campaign?
"Critical," Florida Republican Chairman Tom Slade said. "This election campaign may very well rest on the outcome of the debates."

His assessment reflected the failure of the Dole campaign so far to ignite public interest. But there was a glimmer of good news for the candidate in the latest CNN/USA Today/Gallup poll. It showed a slight tightening of the race, with Clinton ahead by 10 percentage points, 49 percent to 39 percent.

In the same poll, Reform Party candidate Ross Perot, who is seeking a court order to get into the debates, had 6 percent backing from the 737 likely voters surveyed. The poll had a margin of error of plus or minus four percentage points.
The gap between Clinton and Dole was the poll's slimmest. On Sept. 12, it showed a yawning 23-percentage-point gap between the candidates.
Reporters were kept away from the beachfront high-rise housing the condominium owned by Dole's wife, Elizabeth, and her brother.

Dole flew to Florida after a campaign swing through Illinois, Michigan, Ohio, Missouri and Iowa. On Thursday he wooed elderly voters in West Palm Beach with an assurance he would not harm the Medicare health care programme for the aged.
He charged that Clinton was trying to frighten older voters, who make up about 23 percent of the population in a state vital to Dole's chances in the Nov. 5 election.
Florida has 25 electoral votes, nearly 10 percent of the 270 needed to win. It has been a Republican stronghold in presidential elections since 1976.
